claim: Bacteria in biofilms secrete potassium ions to attract free swimming cells.
source: Bacteria in biofilms secrete potassium ions to attract free swimming cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon that motivates the study.

claim: Escherichia coli can rapidly accumulate in regions of high potassium concentration on the order of millimoles.
source: Here, using a microfluidic device, we found that Escherichia coli can rapidly accumulate in regions of high potassium concentration on the order of millimoles.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data from microfluidic device measurements.

claim: The response of E. coli to potassium resulted from the chemotaxis signaling pathway.
source: Using a bead assay, we measured the dynamic response of individual flagellar motors to stepwise changes in potassium concentration, finding that the response resulted from the chemotaxis signaling pathway.
evidence: This is supported by bead assay measurements showing motor CW bias response and lack of response in chemotaxis-defective strains.

claim: The chemotaxis pathway exhibited a sensitive response and fast adaptation to potassium.
source: To characterize the chemotactic response to potassium, we measured the dose–response curve and adaptation kinetics via an Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) assay, finding that the chemotaxis pathway exhibited a sensitive response and fast adaptation to potassium.
evidence: This is supported by FRET assay measurements of dose-response curves and adaptation kinetics.

claim: Tar receptors exhibit a biphasic response to potassium.
source: Tar receptors exhibit a biphasic response, whereas Tsr receptors respond to potassium as an attractant.
evidence: This is supported by FRET measurements in Tar-only mutant strains.

claim: Tsr receptors respond to potassium as an attractant.
source: Tar receptors exhibit a biphasic response, whereas Tsr receptors respond to potassium as an attractant.
evidence: This is supported by FRET measurements in Tsr-only mutant strains.

claim: The different responses of Tar and Tsr receptors to potassium were consistent with the responses of the two receptors to intracellular pH changes.
source: These different responses were consistent with the responses of the two receptors to intracellular pH changes.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with known pH responses and measurements with sodium benzoate.

claim: Potassium ions play a critical role in maintaining the osmotic pressure, pH value and membrane potential of bacterial cells.
source: In prokaryotes, such as bacteria, potassium ions play a critical role in maintaining the osmotic pressure, pH value and membrane potential of cells (Ballal et al., 2007; Epstein, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both the expression of genes and the activities of enzymes are regulated by potassium ions.
source: In addition, both the expression of genes and the activities of enzymes are also regulated by potassium ions (Ali et al., 2017; Ballal et al., 2007; Epstein, 2003; Nanatani et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bacteria sense and respond to chemicals via the chemotaxis signaling pathway.
source: Bacteria sense and respond to chemicals via the chemotaxis signaling pathway.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial chemotaxis.

claim: In Escherichia coli, chemo stimuli are detected by transmembrane receptors.
source: In Escherichia coli, chemo stimuli are detected by transmembrane receptors (Bray et al., 1998; Endres et al., 2008; Homma et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The sensed signal is transmitted to the associated cytoplasmic histidine kinase CheA, affecting its autophosphorylation.
source: The sensed signal is then transmitted to the associated cytoplasmic histidine kinase CheA, affecting its autophosphorylation (Li and Hazelbauer, 2011; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CheA transfers its phosphoryl group to the response regulator CheY and the methylesterase CheB, yielding CheY-P and CheB-P, respectively.
source: CheA transfers its phosphoryl group to the response regulator CheY and the methylesterase CheB, yielding CheY-P and CheB-P, respectively (Bren and Eisenbach, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CheY-P binds to the base of the flagellar motor, increasing the probability of motor rotating clockwise (CW), namely motor CW bias, and thus increasing the cell tumble frequency.
source: CheY-P binds to the base of the flagellar motor, increasing the probability of motor rotating clockwise (CW), namely motor CW bias, and thus increasing the cell tumble frequency (Dyer and Dahlquist, 2006; Lam et al., 2013; van Albada and Ten Wolde, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The phosphatase CheZ binds to CheY-P and accelerates its dephosphorylation.
source: The phosphatase CheZ binds to CheY-P and accelerates its dephosphorylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the chemotaxis signaling pathway.

claim: CheB-P and CheR demethylate and methylate the receptors, respectively, to accomplish robust adaptation in chemotaxis.
source: CheB-P and CheR demethylate and methylate the receptors, respectively, to accomplish robust adaptation in chemotaxis (Djordjevic and Stock, 1997; Djordjevic and Stock, 1998; Levin et al., 2002; Lupas and Stock, 1989; Lybarger and Maddock, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MeAsp and serine can bind to the periplasmic domain of the corresponding receptor directly and modify kinase activity.
source: The former suggests that the ligand can bind to the periplasmic domain of the corresponding receptor directly and modify kinase activity, such as MeAsp and serine (Neumann et al., 2010; Tajima et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Maltose is sensed by the Tar receptor with the help of periplasmic maltose-binding protein.
source: The latter requires the help of binding proteins, such as maltose sensed by the Tar receptor with the help of periplasmic maltose-binding protein (Brass and Manson, 1984), and peptides sensed by the Tap receptor with the help of peptide-binding proteins (Manson et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Peptides are sensed by the Tap receptor with the help of peptide-binding proteins.
source: The latter requires the help of binding proteins, such as maltose sensed by the Tar receptor with the help of periplasmic maltose-binding protein (Brass and Manson, 1984), and peptides sensed by the Tap receptor with the help of peptide-binding proteins (Manson et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bacteria in biofilms secrete potassium into their surroundings through ion channels on the cell membrane, thereby affecting the behavior of distant free bacteria and attracting them.
source: It was discovered recently that bacteria in biofilms secrete potassium into their surroundings through ion channels on the cell membrane, thereby affecting the behavior of distant free bacteria and attracting them (Humphries et al., 2017; Prindle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Wild-type E. coli exhibited significant movement toward the area of high concentration in a linear concentration gradient of potassium chloride.
source: According to our results, the wild-type strain exhibited significant movement toward the area of high concentration in a linear concentration gradient of potassium chloride, which was similar to its chemotaxis in a typical attractant concentration gradient (Jiang et al., 2010; Kalinin et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2022; Son et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by microfluidic device measurements and comparison with known attractant responses.

claim: The drift velocity of wild-type E. coli in a linear potassium gradient is 0.45 ± 0.02 μm/s.
source: For wild-type E. coli with vs = 53.2 μm2/s (Wu et al., 2006), we obtained a drift velocity vd = 0.45 ± 0.02 μm/s.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data using the fitted exponential decay constant.

claim: A sudden change in membrane potential in E. coli would result in a reverse change in the transmembrane proton concentration difference, thus keeping PMF virtually constant.
source: However, earlier studies found that a sudden change in membrane potential in E. coli would result in a reverse change in the transmembrane proton concentration difference, thus keeping PMF virtually constant (Bakker and Mangerich, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The motor speed remained constant during the response to potassium, confirming that the PMF remained constant.
source: However, the motor speed remained constant during this process, confirming that the PMF remained constant, which was different from the osmotaxis response of motors.
evidence: This is supported by bead assay measurements showing constant motor speed.

claim: The chemotaxis-defective strain exhibited no response to 30 mM potassium chloride for either CW bias or speed.
source: We performed further experiments with the chemotaxis-defective strain (HCB901-pBES38). The average result of 22 motors exhibited no response to 30 mM potassium chloride for either CW bias or speed (Figure 2D), especially on the time scale of the chemotactic response as seen in the wild-type cells.
evidence: This is supported by bead assay measurements with chemotaxis-defective strain.

claim: The response of motor CW bias to potassium resulted from the upstream chemotaxis signaling pathway.
source: These results confirmed that the CW bias response of the motor to potassium resulted from the upstream chemotaxis signaling pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of response in chemotaxis-defective strains and the constant PMF.

claim: 30 mM KCl resulted in a larger response and faster adaptation compared to 100 μM MeAsp.
source: Compared with 100 μM MeAsp, 30 mM KCl resulted in a larger response and faster adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by FRET assay measurements comparing responses to KCl and MeAsp.

claim: The chemotactic signal exhibits an imprecise adaptation to potassium.
source: Moreover, the chemotactic signal exhibits an imprecise adaptation.
evidence: This is observed in FRET measurements, though later corrected for pH effects.

claim: The chemotactic response mainly resulted from potassium ions rather than chloride ions.
source: Thus, the chemotactic response mainly resulted from potassium ions rather than chloride ions.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of responses to KCl and K2SO4 at equivalent potassium concentrations.

claim: Changes in osmotic pressure caused by a change in ion concentration on the millimole scale can lead to chemotactic responses in E. coli by altering the interaction between receptors.
source: Earlier studies have shown that changes in osmotic pressure caused by a change in ion concentration on the millimole scale can also lead to chemotactic responses in E. coli by altering the interaction between receptors (Vaknin and Berg, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: 60 mM sucrose induced a repellent-like response.
source: In our measurements, 60 mM sucrose induced a repellent-like response, which is consistent with previous work (Vaknin and Berg, 2006), whereas 30 mM KCl induced an attractant response.
evidence: This is supported by FRET measurements and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The chemotactic response of E. coli to KCl did not result from osmotaxis.
source: Thus, the chemotactic response of E. coli to KCl did not result from osmotaxis.
evidence: This is inferred from the opposite responses to KCl and sucrose at equivalent osmotic pressure.

claim: The response to 30 mM KCl was 1.79 ± 0.10 times as large as that to 100 μM MeAsp (before pH correction).
source: The response to 30 mM KCl was 1.79 ± 0.10 times as large as that to 100 μM MeAsp, while the response to 60 mM sucrose was −0.30 ± 0.05 times as large as that to 100 μM MeAsp.
evidence: This is calculated from FRET measurements before pH correction.

claim: The response to 60 mM sucrose was −0.30 ± 0.05 times as large as that to 100 μM MeAsp.
source: The response to 30 mM KCl was 1.79 ± 0.10 times as large as that to 100 μM MeAsp, while the response to 60 mM sucrose was −0.30 ± 0.05 times as large as that to 100 μM MeAsp.
evidence: This is calculated from FRET measurements.

claim: The fitted Hill coefficient for the dose-response curve to potassium was 0.53 ± 0.04 (before pH correction).
source: The fitted Hill coefficient was 0.53 ± 0.04.
evidence: This is obtained by fitting experimental dose-response data before pH correction.

claim: The fitted Hill coefficient for the dose-response curve to potassium was 0.88 ± 0.14 (after pH correction).
source: However, this value was revised to 0.88 ± 0.14 when we corrected the FRET responses for the pH effects on the brightness of eCFP and eYFP (the blue dots and red solid line).
evidence: This is obtained by fitting experimental dose-response data after pH correction.

claim: The concentration for half-maximal response (K0.5) to potassium was 0.64 ± 0.12 mM (before pH correction).
source: The concentration for half-maximal response (K0.5) was 0.64 ± 0.12 mM before correction and 0.33 ± 0.06 mM after correction.
evidence: This is obtained by fitting experimental dose-response data before pH correction.

claim: The concentration for half-maximal response (K0.5) to potassium was 0.33 ± 0.06 mM (after pH correction).
source: The concentration for half-maximal response (K0.5) was 0.64 ± 0.12 mM before correction and 0.33 ± 0.06 mM after correction.
evidence: This is obtained by fitting experimental dose-response data after pH correction.

claim: E. coli responds sensitively and adapts quickly to potassium chloride in a range of 0.01–100 mM.
source: According to our measurements, E. coli responds sensitively (with a small K0.5) and adapts quickly to potassium chloride in a range of 0.01–100 mM.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response and adaptation kinetics measurements.

claim: The intracellular pH of the wild-type strain increases immediately upon addition of 30 mM KCl.
source: The intracellular pH of the wild-type strain (HCB33-pTrc99a_pHlourin2) increases immediately upon addition of 30 mM KCl.
evidence: This is supported by measurements using pH-sensitive fluorescent protein pHlourin2.

claim: The increase in the extracellular concentration of potassium leads to an increase in the intracellular pH.
source: Our results indicated that the increase in the extracellular concentration of potassium leads to an increase in the intracellular pH.
evidence: This is supported by pH measurements with pHlourin2.

claim: Tar and Tsr mediate opposite responses to the changes in intracellular pH.
source: It was reported that Tar and Tsr mediate opposite responses to the changes in intracellular pH (Krikos et al., 1985; Umemura et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Tsr-only strain exhibited an attractant response to potassium.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, four different concentrations of KCl were added and removed successively, and the kinases activity of the Tsr-only strain exhibited an attractant response.
evidence: This is supported by FRET measurements in Tsr-only mutant strain.

claim: The Tar-only strain exhibited a biphasic response to potassium, with kinase activity increasing sharply and then decreasing rapidly below the pre-stimulus level upon addition of potassium.
source: In contrast, the Tar-only strain exhibited a biphasic response, with kinase activity increasing sharply and then decreasing rapidly below the pre-stimulus level upon addition of potassium (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by FRET measurements in Tar-only mutant strain.

claim: The different responses of the Tar- and Tsr-only strains to potassium were consistent with the responses to the increase in intracellular pH.
source: Therefore, the different responses of the Tar- and Tsr-only strains to potassium were consistent with the responses to the increase in intracellular pH.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with known pH responses and measurements with sodium benzoate.

claim: Both major receptors exhibited imprecise adaptation to stepwise addition of potassium.
source: We noted that both major receptors exhibited imprecise adaptation to stepwise addition of potassium.
evidence: This is observed in FRET measurements of Tar-only and Tsr-only strains.

claim: The imprecise adaptation seen for the wild-type, Tar-only, and Tsr-only strains was not due to chemosensing.
source: This indicated that the imprecise adaptation seen for the wild-type, Tar-only, and Tsr-only strains was not due to chemosensing.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar response in the no-receptor strain.

claim: The apparent imprecise adaptation was due to the differential change in eCFP and eYFP brightness when the cytoplasmic pH changed.
source: As the solution pH affects the brightness of fluorescent proteins, we hypothesize that this apparent imprecise adaptation was due to the differential change in eCFP and eYFP brightness when the cytoplasmic pH changed.
evidence: This is supported by YFP bleaching experiments showing similar CFP response before and after bleaching.

claim: The corrected response magnitude to 30 mM KCl is similar to that of 100 μM MeAsp, being 1.06 ± 0.10 times as large.
source: The corrected response magnitude to 30 mM KCl is similar to that of 100 μM MeAsp, being 1.06 ± 0.10 times as large, as shown by the red bar in Figure 3C.
evidence: This is calculated from pH-corrected FRET measurements.

claim: The FRET signal exhibits over-adaptation when recalculated by correcting the CFP and YFP channels for pH effects.
source: The FRET signal also exhibits over-adaptation, similar to the bead assay, when we recalculated the response by correcting the CFP and YFP channels.
evidence: This is observed in pH-corrected FRET measurements.

claim: The fitted Hill coefficient for the pH-corrected dose-response curve is 0.88 ± 0.14, which is close to the response to MeAsp (~1.2).
source: The fitted Hill coefficient for the dose–response curve is 0.88 ± 0.14 (mean ± standard deviation [SD]), which is close to the response to MeAsp (~1.2) (Sourjik and Berg, 2002b), and the concentration for half-maximal response (K0.5) was 0.33 ± 0.06 mM (mean ± SD).
evidence: This is obtained by fitting pH-corrected dose-response data and comparing with literature values.

claim: The wild-type strain exhibits a similar response to the Tsr-only strain due to the larger amount of Tsr than Tar receptors.
source: The wild-type strain exhibits a similar response to the Tsr-only strain due to the larger amount of Tsr than Tar receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of responses and known receptor expression levels.

claim: E. coli cells can be periodically attracted by the biofilm based on the potassium sensing mechanism.
source: Based on the potassium sensing mechanism we established here, we performed stochastic simulation of bacterial taxis in a biofilm-produced potassium gradient, demonstrating that E. coli cells can be periodically attracted by the biofilm.
evidence: This is demonstrated by computational simulation using parameters from experimental measurements.

claim: The oscillation of E. coli cell displacement lags the potassium source by 11.7 ± 0.5, 14.7 ± 0.7, 14.8 ± 0.9, and 14.2 ± 1.0 min for driving periods of 1, 2, 3, and 4 hr, respectively.
source: Specifically, we found that the oscillation of E. coli cell displacement lags the potassium source by 11.7 ± 0.5, 14.7 ± 0.7, 14.8 ± 0.9, and 14.2 ± 1.0 min (mean ± SD) for driving periods of 1, 2, 3, and 4 hr, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from computational simulations.

claim: The simulated lag times closely resemble the 9–35 min lag observed in biofilm experiments for B. subtilis and P. aeruginosa.
source: Remarkably, these values closely resemble the 9–35 min lag observed in biofilm experiments for B. subtilis and P. aeruginosa (Humphries et al., 2017), despite the potential variations in the potassium sensing mechanisms among these bacterial species.
evidence: This is a comparison between simulation results and experimental observations from literature.

claim: E. coli had a very sensitive response to potassium ions and could sense weak changes in potassium concentration.
source: This showed that E. coli had a very sensitive response to potassium ions and could sense weak changes in potassium concentration.
evidence: This is inferred from the low K0.5 value measured in dose-response experiments.

claim: E. coli adapts quickly to potassium concentration changes in the range of 0.01–100 mM, which promotes cell localization to the peak of a potassium concentration profile.
source: We also found that E. coli adapts quickly to potassium concentration changes in the range of 0.01–100 mM, which promotes cell localization to the peak of a potassium concentration profile.
evidence: This is inferred from adaptation kinetics measurements.

claim: Addition of potassium decreases the membrane potential and thus increases the intracellular pH while keeping the PMF unchanged.
source: While keeping the PMF unchanged, addition of potassium decreases the membrane potential and thus increases the intracellular pH.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pH measurements and motor speed measurements.

claim: The differential responses of the Tsr and Tar receptors to potassium may be a strategy by which bacteria adjust their response to potassium at different growth stages during which bacteria express different ratios of Tsr to Tar receptors.
source: The differential responses of the Tsr and Tar receptors to potassium may be a strategy by which bacteria adjust their response to potassium at different growth stages during which bacteria express different ratios of Tsr to Tar receptors (Kalinin et al., 2010; Yang and Sourjik, 2012).
evidence: This is speculation based on known receptor expression patterns at different growth stages.

claim: For the growth stage used in the measurements, the amount of Tsr was more than that of Tar in the wild-type strain, so the response to potassium was dominated by Tsr.
source: For the growth stage used in our measurements here, the amount of Tsr was more than that of Tar in the wild-type strain (Li and Hazelbauer, 2004), so the response to potassium was dominated by Tsr.
evidence: This is inferred from known receptor expression levels and observed response patterns.

claim: The Tar-only strain shows a repellent response to stepwise addition of low concentrations of potassium, specifically less than 10 mM.
source: This strain shows a repellent response to stepwise addition of low concentrations of potassium, specifically less than 10 mM.
evidence: This is observed in FRET measurements of Tar-only strain.

claim: The Tar-only strain exhibits a biphasic response to high potassium concentrations of 10 mM and above.
source: Interestingly, it exhibits a biphasic response to high potassium concentrations of 10 mM and above.
evidence: This is observed in FRET measurements of Tar-only strain.

claim: The biphasic response of Tar-only strain to high potassium concentrations might result from additional pH effects on the activity of intracellular enzymes such as CheRB and CheA.
source: This biphasic response might result from additional pH effects on the activity of intracellular enzymes such as CheRB and CheA (Conley et al., 1994), which may have a different timescale and response from the Tar receptor.
evidence: This is speculation based on known pH effects on enzyme activity.

claim: The phase delay between the mean x-position and the potassium source decreases significantly with the increase of driving period.
source: We found that the phase delay decreases significantly with the increase of driving period, a trend that is consistent with previous experimental observations in the biofilm (Humphries et al., 2017).
evidence: This is observed in computational simulations and compared with experimental observations.

claim: The lag time result was not affected by the specific value of L0.
source: Notably, this result was not affected by the specific value of L0 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulations with different L0 values.

claim: E. coli senses the concentration change of extracellular potassium ions sensitively via the chemotaxis signaling pathway.
source: Here, we found that E. coli senses the concentration change of extracellular potassium ions sensitively via the chemotaxis signaling pathway, and this chemotactic sensing is achieved through changes in intracellular pH.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by multiple experimental measurements.

claim: The chemotactic sensing of potassium is achieved through changes in intracellular pH.
source: Here, we found that E. coli senses the concentration change of extracellular potassium ions sensitively via the chemotaxis signaling pathway, and this chemotactic sensing is achieved through changes in intracellular pH.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by pH measurements and receptor-specific responses.

claim: The attractant response to potassium was independent of the osmolality response.
source: This suggested that the attractant response to potassium was independent of the osmolality response.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of responses to KCl and sucrose at equivalent osmotic pressure.

claim: The distribution of cells is exponential at steady state in a linear potassium gradient, similar to the results of logarithmic chemotactic sensing in a linear MeAsp gradient.
source: We found that the distribution of cells is exponential at steady state, similar to the results of logarithmic chemotactic sensing in a linear MeAsp gradient (Kalinin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is observed in microfluidic experiments and compared with previous literature.

claim: The fitted exponential decay constant equals vd/vs, where vd and vs denote the drift velocity and cell motility constant, respectively.
source: As reported previously (Kalinin et al., 2009), the fitted exponential decay constant equals vd/vs, where vd and vs denote the drift velocity and cell motility constant, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous literature.

claim: The CW bias is positively correlated with the intracellular concentration of CheY-P.
source: The CW bias is positively correlated with the intracellular concentration of CheY-P (Cluzel et al., 2000), and the rotational speed is proportional to the PMF (Gabel and Berg, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous literature.

claim: The rotational speed is proportional to the PMF.
source: The CW bias is positively correlated with the intracellular concentration of CheY-P (Cluzel et al., 2000), and the rotational speed is proportional to the PMF (Gabel and Berg, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous literature.

claim: The CW bias decreased upon addition of potassium chloride, and then it adapted to a higher level than the pre-stimulus value.
source: The CW bias decreased upon addition of potassium chloride, and then it adapted to a higher level than the pre-stimulus value.
evidence: This is observed in bead assay measurements.

claim: The over adaptation in CW bias response to potassium was similar to the response of CW bias to sucrose in osomotaxis.
source: Such over adaptation was similar to the response of CW bias to sucrose in osomotaxis (Rosko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature on osmotaxis.

claim: 10 mM KCl and 5 mM K2SO4 induce similar chemotactic responses.
source: To exclude the effect of chloride ion, we quantitatively compared the response of the chemotactic signal to 10 mM KCl and 5 mM K2SO4, both of which contain 10 mM potassium ion with or without chloride ion. As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, they induce similar responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET measurements comparing KCl and K2SO4.

claim: The response of CW bias to 15 mM K2SO4 exhibited an attractant response, characterized by a decreased CW bias upon the addition of K2SO4, followed by an over-adaptation that is qualitatively similar to the response to 30 mM KCl.
source: The response of CW bias to 15 mM K2SO4 exhibited an attractant response, characterized by a decreased CW bias upon the addition of K2SO4, followed by an over-adaptation that is qualitatively similar to the response to 30 mM KCl.
evidence: This is observed in bead assay measurements comparing K2SO4 and KCl.

claim: A high concentration of potassium chloride (300 mM) could attract swimming cells.
source: It has been reported that potassium ions work as a communication agent in swarms and biofilms for both Bacillus subtilis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. A high concentration of potassium chloride (300 mM) could attract swimming cells (Humphries et al., 2017; Prindle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is reported in previous literature.

claim: Potassium ions work as a communication agent in swarms and biofilms for both Bacillus subtilis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: It has been reported that potassium ions work as a communication agent in swarms and biofilms for both Bacillus subtilis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. A high concentration of potassium chloride (300 mM) could attract swimming cells (Humphries et al., 2017; Prindle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is reported in previous literature.

claim: The absolute value of the transmembrane electrical potential will decrease when the concentration of extracellular potassium increases.
source: The absolute value of the transmembrane electrical potential will decrease when the concentration of extracellular potassium increases.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of membrane potential.

claim: Potassium deficiency can affect many biological functions, such as human heartbeat and photosynthesis and respiration of plants.
source: Potassium deficiency can affect many biological functions, such as human heartbeat (Zacchia et al., 2016) and photosynthesis and respiration of plants (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Potassium ions are a major component in establishing the resting membrane potential and thus ensure proper function of the muscles and nerves.
source: Potassium ions are a major component in establishing the resting membrane potential and thus ensure proper function of the muscles and nerves.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge.

claim: Potassium is an important ion in the normal physiological process of organisms.
source: Potassium is an important ion in the normal physiological process of organisms (Gründling, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.
